catalog_quote: Nasals preceding consonants are homorganic. In initial position, nasals are usually tone-bearing, but in word-medial position they are usually not, except when the word is an old compound. Consonants followed by –r, -ɽ and –l are extremely common as are labialisation and palatalisation. 3.3 Tones Ninzo has three level tones and a rising and falling tone, represented as follows; High ˊ / Mid Unmarked / Low ˋ / Rising ˇ / Falling ˆ 4. Morphology 4.1 Nouns The dominant procedure for forming plurals is alternation of V- prefixes. The tone on these prefixes is highly variable and may well be driven by stem tones. ... Many words have unproductive prefixes and singular and plural is now marked only by tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ninzo is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) plus rising and falling contours; the source makes no statement at all about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress discussion); tone on noun prefixes said to be 'highly variable and may well be driven by stem tones' (4.1)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statement only; lexical citation forms in a wordlist. The document never uses the words 'stress' or 'accent'. This is a tone-only description, not a stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench 2011 describes the Fadan Wate lect of Ninzo (Kaduna State), partly a recension of Hörner 1980 rechecked in 1995; 'Ninzam' (older literature, Hörner, Gerhardt, Greenberg's Plateau 4) = Ninzo, glottocode ninz1246, ISO nin. Blench lists seven dialect groups (Amar Dogo, Amar Lada, Amar Tita, Ancha, Kwasa, Sambe, Fadan Wate) with 'quite marked' differences; Buhari 2025 misassigns Ninzo to 'Western Kainji' but treats the same language.
